claim: Centrioles play critical roles in organizing the assembly of the mitotic spindle.
source: Centrioles play critical roles in organizing the assembly of the mitotic spindle and templating the formation of primary cilia.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Centrioles template the formation of primary cilia.
source: Centrioles play critical roles in organizing the assembly of the mitotic spindle and templating the formation of primary cilia.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Centriole duplication occurs once per cell cycle.
source: Centriole duplication occurs once per cell cycle and is regulated by Polo-like kinase 4 (PLK4).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Centriole duplication is regulated by Polo-like kinase 4 (PLK4).
source: Centriole duplication occurs once per cell cycle and is regulated by Polo-like kinase 4 (PLK4).
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: PLK4 phosphorylates STIL on a conserved site, S428.
source: Here, we show that PLK4 phosphorylates its centriole substrate STIL on a conserved site, S428, to promote STIL binding to CPAP.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PLK4 phosphorylation of STIL S428 promotes STIL binding to CPAP.
source: Here, we show that PLK4 phosphorylates its centriole substrate STIL on a conserved site, S428, to promote STIL binding to CPAP.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The phospho-dependent binding interaction between STIL and CPAP is conserved in Drosophila.
source: This phospho-dependent binding interaction is conserved in Drosophila and facilitates the stable incorporation of both STIL and CPAP into the centriole.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Drosophila S2 cells shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The phospho-dependent binding interaction between STIL and CPAP facilitates the stable incorporation of both STIL and CPAP into the centriole.
source: This phospho-dependent binding interaction is conserved in Drosophila and facilitates the stable incorporation of both STIL and CPAP into the centriole.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Procentriole assembly requires PLK4 to phosphorylate STIL in two different regions.
source: We propose that procentriole assembly requires PLK4 to phosphorylate STIL in two different regions: phosphorylation of residues in the STAN motif allow STIL to bind SAS6 and initiate cartwheel assembly, while phosphorylation of S428 promotes the binding of STIL to CPAP, linking the cartwheel to microtubules of the centriole wall.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation of residues in the STAN motif of STIL allows STIL to bind SAS6 and initiate cartwheel assembly.
source: We propose that procentriole assembly requires PLK4 to phosphorylate STIL in two different regions: phosphorylation of residues in the STAN motif allow STIL to bind SAS6 and initiate cartwheel assembly, while phosphorylation of S428 promotes the binding of STIL to CPAP, linking the cartwheel to microtubules of the centriole wall.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript and data in Figure 3.

claim: Phosphorylation of STIL S428 promotes the binding of STIL to CPAP, linking the cartwheel to microtubules of the centriole wall.
source: We propose that procentriole assembly requires PLK4 to phosphorylate STIL in two different regions: phosphorylation of residues in the STAN motif allow STIL to bind SAS6 and initiate cartwheel assembly, while phosphorylation of S428 promotes the binding of STIL to CPAP, linking the cartwheel to microtubules of the centriole wall.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 2, 3, 4, and 6.

claim: Centrosomes nucleate the formation of the microtubule cytoskeleton in interphase cells.
source: Centrosomes nucleate the formation of the microtubule cytoskeleton in interphase cells and form the poles of the mitotic spindle during cell division.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology supported by citations (Nigg and Holland, 2018; Gönczy, 2012).

claim: Centrosomes form the poles of the mitotic spindle during cell division.
source: Centrosomes nucleate the formation of the microtubule cytoskeleton in interphase cells and form the poles of the mitotic spindle during cell division.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology supported by citations (Nigg and Holland, 2018; Gönczy, 2012).

claim: In quiescent cells, centrioles dock at the plasma membrane and act as basal bodies that template the formation of cilia and flagella.
source: In quiescent cells, centrioles dock at the plasma membrane and act as basal bodies that template the formation of cilia and flagella (Breslow and Holland, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Breslow and Holland, 2019).

claim: Centriole duplication begins at the G1-S phase transition.
source: Centriole duplication begins at the G1-S phase transition when a new procentriole grows perpendicularly from a single site at the proximal end of each of the two parent centrioles.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: A new procentriole grows perpendicularly from a single site at the proximal end of each of the two parent centrioles.
source: Centriole duplication begins at the G1-S phase transition when a new procentriole grows perpendicularly from a single site at the proximal end of each of the two parent centrioles.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: In late G2 phase, the two centriole pairs separate and increase PCM recruitment to promote the formation of the mitotic spindle.
source: In late G2 phase, the two centriole pairs separate and increase PCM recruitment to promote the formation of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: At the end of mitosis, the centrosomes are equally partitioned so that each daughter cell inherits a pair of centrioles.
source: At the end of mitosis, the centrosomes are equally partitioned so that each daughter cell inherits a pair of centrioles.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Defects in centriole biogenesis can result in the formation of supernumerary centrosomes.
source: Defects in centriole biogenesis can result in the formation of supernumerary centrosomes which promote mitotic errors that can contribute to tumorigenesis (Levine et al., 2017; Levine and Holland, 2018; Basto et al., 2008; Serçin et al., 2016; Coelho et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Supernumerary centrosomes promote mitotic errors that can contribute to tumorigenesis.
source: Defects in centriole biogenesis can result in the formation of supernumerary centrosomes which promote mitotic errors that can contribute to tumorigenesis (Levine et al., 2017; Levine and Holland, 2018; Basto et al., 2008; Serçin et al., 2016; Coelho et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutations in centriole proteins are linked to growth retardation syndromes and autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (MPCH) in human patients.
source: Moreover, mutations in centriole proteins are linked to growth retardation syndromes and autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (MPCH) in human patients (Nigg and Raff, 2009; Chavali et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Nigg and Raff, 2009; Chavali et al., 2014).

claim: The initiation of centriole duplication requires a conserved set of five core proteins: PLK4, CEP192, CPAP, STIL and SAS6.
source: The initiation of centriole duplication requires a conserved set of five core proteins: PLK4 (ZYG-1 in C. elegans), CEP192 (SPD-2 in C. elegans and Spd-2 in Drosophila), CPAP (also known as CENPJ, SAS-4 in C.elegans and Sas-4 in Drosophila), STIL (SAS-5 in C. elegans and Ana-2 in Drosophila) and SAS6 (Leidel et al., 2005; Leidel and Gönczy, 2003; Dammermann et al., 2004; Delattre et al., 2004; Kemp et al., 2004; O'Connell et al., 2001; Pelletier et al., 2004; Kirkham et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: PLK4 has been identified as the central regulator of centriole assembly.
source: Of these components, PLK4 has been identified as the central regulator of centriole assembly (Habedanck et al., 2005; Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Habedanck et al., 2005; Bettencourt-Dias et al., 2005).

claim: In mammalian cells, PLK4 is recruited to the centriole during G1 phase through binding to its centriole receptors CEP152 and CEP192.
source: In mammalian cells, PLK4 is recruited to the centriole during G1 phase through binding to its centriole receptors CEP152 and CEP192, which encircle the proximal end of the parent centriole (Cizmecioglu et al., 2010; Hatch et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013; Park et al., 2014; Sonnen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CEP152 and CEP192 encircle the proximal end of the parent centriole.
source: In mammalian cells, PLK4 is recruited to the centriole during G1 phase through binding to its centriole receptors CEP152 and CEP192, which encircle the proximal end of the parent centriole (Cizmecioglu et al., 2010; Hatch et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013; Park et al., 2014; Sonnen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: At G1-S phase transition, PLK4 transforms from a ring-like localization to a single focus on the wall of the parent centriole that marks the site of procentriole formation.
source: At G1-S phase transition, PLK4 transforms from a ring-like localization to a single focus on the wall of the parent centriole that marks the site of procentriole formation (Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; Sonnen et al., 2012; Dzhindzhev et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The ring-to-dot transformation of PLK4 bears features of a symmetry breaking reaction.
source: This transition bears features of a symmetry breaking reaction and can be recreated in silico using two positive feedback loops that act on PLK4 (Goryachev and Leda, 2017; Leda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Goryachev and Leda, 2017; Leda et al., 2018).

claim: The ring-to-dot transformation of PLK4 can be recreated in silico using two positive feedback loops that act on PLK4.
source: This transition bears features of a symmetry breaking reaction and can be recreated in silico using two positive feedback loops that act on PLK4 (Goryachev and Leda, 2017; Leda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Goryachev and Leda, 2017; Leda et al., 2018).

claim: Binding of PLK4 to its centriole substrate STIL promotes activation of the kinase.
source: Binding of PLK4 to its centriole substrate STIL promotes activation of the kinase and is required for its ring-to-dot transformation (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Lopes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Lopes et al., 2015).

claim: Binding of PLK4 to STIL is required for PLK4's ring-to-dot transformation.
source: Binding of PLK4 to its centriole substrate STIL promotes activation of the kinase and is required for its ring-to-dot transformation (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Lopes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Lopes et al., 2015).

claim: PLK4 phosphorylates STIL in a conserved STAN motif to promote the binding and recruitment of SAS6.
source: PLK4 phosphorylates STIL in a conserved STAN motif to promote the binding and recruitment of SAS6 (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Dzhindzhev et al., 2014; Kratz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: SAS6 homo-oligomerizes to organize the central cartwheel.
source: SAS6 homo-oligomerizes to organize the central cartwheel, a stack of ring-like assemblies with nine-fold symmetry that provides the structural foundation for the procentriole (Kitagawa et al., 2011a; van Breugel et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2014; Cottee et al., 2015; Guichard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The central cartwheel is a stack of ring-like assemblies with nine-fold symmetry that provides the structural foundation for the procentriole.
source: SAS6 homo-oligomerizes to organize the central cartwheel, a stack of ring-like assemblies with nine-fold symmetry that provides the structural foundation for the procentriole (Kitagawa et al., 2011a; van Breugel et al., 2011; van Breugel et al., 2014; Cottee et al., 2015; Guichard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CPAP plays a critical role in the formation and stabilization of the triplet microtubule blades that make up the procentriole wall.
source: Following cartwheel assembly, the centriole protein CPAP plays a critical role in the formation and stabilization of the triplet microtubule blades that make up the procentriole wall.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the context and citations in the manuscript.

claim: CPAP interacts with multiple centriole proteins including STIL, CEP152, CEP120, CEP135, and Centrobin.
source: CPAP interacts with multiple centriole proteins including STIL (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Vulprecht et al., 2012), CEP152 (Cizmecioglu et al., 2010; Dzhindzhev et al., 2010), CEP120 (Lin et al., 2013a), CEP135 (Lin et al., 2013b), and Centrobin (Gudi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The C-terminal TCP domain of CPAP directly binds to a highly conserved PRP motif in STIL.
source: The C-terminal TCP domain of CPAP directly binds to a highly conserved PRP motif in STIL (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Vulprecht et al., 2012), while the N-terminal domain of CPAP interacts with α/β-tubulin heterodimers (Sharma et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2016; Hung et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Vulprecht et al., 2012).

claim: The N-terminal domain of CPAP interacts with α/β-tubulin heterodimers.
source: The C-terminal TCP domain of CPAP directly binds to a highly conserved PRP motif in STIL (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Vulprecht et al., 2012), while the N-terminal domain of CPAP interacts with α/β-tubulin heterodimers (Sharma et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2016; Hung et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Sharma et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2016; Hung et al., 2004).

claim: CPAP acts as a molecular link between the cartwheel and the triplet microtubule blades of the centriole wall.
source: These interactions allow CPAP to act as a molecular link between the cartwheel and the triplet microtubule blades of the centriole wall.
evidence: This is inferred from the interactions described and supported by the context.

claim: An MCPH mutation in the CPAP TCP domain weakens the STIL-CPAP interaction.
source: Importantly, an MCPH mutation in the CPAP TCP domain weakens the STIL-CPAP interaction, highlighting the importance of this complex in centriole assembly and function (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Bond et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Bond et al., 2005).

claim: CPAP positively regulates centriolar microtubule growth.
source: CPAP positively regulates centriolar microtubule growth and, consequently, overexpression of CPAP leads to the formation of overly long centrioles in human cells (Tang et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Kohlmaier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Tang et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Kohlmaier et al., 2009).

claim: Overexpression of CPAP leads to the formation of overly long centrioles in human cells.
source: CPAP positively regulates centriolar microtubule growth and, consequently, overexpression of CPAP leads to the formation of overly long centrioles in human cells (Tang et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Kohlmaier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Tang et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009; Kohlmaier et al., 2009).

claim: CPAP functions in recruiting PCM, either through the direct tethering of PCM proteins or by recruiting Plk1/Polo which is critical in promoting PCM assembly.
source: In addition to its role in controlling microtubule growth, CPAP also functions in recruiting PCM, either through the direct tethering of PCM proteins or by recruiting Plk1/Polo which is critical in promoting PCM assembly (Zheng et al., 2014; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2011; Chou et al., 2016; Novak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Zheng et al., 2014; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2011; Chou et al., 2016; Novak et al., 2016).

claim: The binding of SAS6 to the STAN motif of STIL is the only interaction known to be controlled by PLK4 kinase activity prior to this study.
source: At present, the binding of SAS6 to the STAN motif of STIL is the only interaction known to be controlled by PLK4 kinase activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The regulation of the SAS6-STIL interaction is conserved in humans and flies.
source: While the regulation of this assembly step is conserved in humans and flies (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Dzhindzhev et al., 2014; Kratz et al., 2015), it is unclear whether this takes place in C. elegans, where ZYG-1/PLK4 directly binds and recruits SAS6 to promote cartwheel assembly (Lettman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Dzhindzhev et al., 2014; Kratz et al., 2015).

claim: In C. elegans, ZYG-1/PLK4 directly binds and recruits SAS6 to promote cartwheel assembly.
source: While the regulation of this assembly step is conserved in humans and flies (Ohta et al., 2014; Moyer et al., 2015; Dzhindzhev et al., 2014; Kratz et al., 2015), it is unclear whether this takes place in C. elegans, where ZYG-1/PLK4 directly binds and recruits SAS6 to promote cartwheel assembly (Lettman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Lettman et al., 2013).

claim: Phosphomimetic mutations in the crucial PLK4 phosphorylation sites in the STAN motif of STIL are functional.
source: Moreover, although phosphomimetic mutations in the crucial PLK4 phosphorylation sites in the STAN motif of STIL are functional, they cannot support centriole duplication in the absence of PLK4 kinase activity (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Kim et al., 2016).

claim: Phosphomimetic mutations in the STAN motif of STIL cannot support centriole duplication in the absence of PLK4 kinase activity.
source: Moreover, although phosphomimetic mutations in the crucial PLK4 phosphorylation sites in the STAN motif of STIL are functional, they cannot support centriole duplication in the absence of PLK4 kinase activity (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Kim et al., 2016).

claim: PLK4 must phosphorylate STIL, or other substrates, at additional sites to promote centriole assembly.
source: This suggests that PLK4 must phosphorylate STIL, or other substrates, at additional sites to promote centriole assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that phosphomimetic mutations in the STAN motif are not sufficient for centriole duplication.

claim: Recent work in Drosophila identified additional PLK4 phosphorylation sites required for centriole biogenesis in the N-terminus of Ana2/STIL.
source: Indeed, recent work in Drosophila identified additional PLK4 phosphorylation sites required for centriole biogenesis in the N-terminus of Ana2/STIL, but exactly how these phosphorylation events contribute to centriole formation remains unclear (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017; McLamarrah et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017; McLamarrah et al., 2018).

claim: Active PLK4 triggers its own degradation.
source: Active PLK4 triggers its own degradation and thus, we used a PLK4∆24 mutant that stabilizes the active kinase by preventing PLK4-induced autodestruction (Holland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Holland et al., 2010).

claim: PLK4∆24 mutant stabilizes the active kinase by preventing PLK4-induced autodestruction.
source: Active PLK4 triggers its own degradation and thus, we used a PLK4∆24 mutant that stabilizes the active kinase by preventing PLK4-induced autodestruction (Holland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Holland et al., 2010).

claim: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry increased the binding of STIL to SAS6 in cells.
source: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry increased the binding of STIL to SAS6 in cells (Figure 1A), but did not increase binding to the STIL-interacting partners RTTN (Chen et al., 2017) or CEP85 (Figure 1B,C) (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Kinase active PLK4 did not increase STIL binding to RTTN.
source: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry increased the binding of STIL to SAS6 in cells (Figure 1A), but did not increase binding to the STIL-interacting partners RTTN (Chen et al., 2017) or CEP85 (Figure 1B,C) (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Kinase active PLK4 did not increase STIL binding to CEP85.
source: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry increased the binding of STIL to SAS6 in cells (Figure 1A), but did not increase binding to the STIL-interacting partners RTTN (Chen et al., 2017) or CEP85 (Figure 1B,C) (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PLK4 kinase activity promoted a robust increase in STIL binding to CPAP.
source: Unexpectedly, we observed that PLK4 kinase activity promoted a robust increase in STIL binding to CPAP, suggesting that PLK4 kinase activity also controls the interaction of CPAP with STIL (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: STIL S428 is highly conserved.
source: Of the 84 in vitro phosphorylation sites we identified on STIL, S428 was of particular interest as it is highly conserved, matches the PLK4 consensus phosphorylation sequence and is positioned close to the known CPAP binding region on STIL (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Cottee et al., 2013; Kettenbach et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2007; Hatzopoulos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: STIL S428 matches the PLK4 consensus phosphorylation sequence.
source: Of the 84 in vitro phosphorylation sites we identified on STIL, S428 was of particular interest as it is highly conserved, matches the PLK4 consensus phosphorylation sequence and is positioned close to the known CPAP binding region on STIL (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Cottee et al., 2013; Kettenbach et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2007; Hatzopoulos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and consensus motif analysis.

claim: STIL S428 is positioned close to the known CPAP binding region on STIL.
source: Of the 84 in vitro phosphorylation sites we identified on STIL, S428 was of particular interest as it is highly conserved, matches the PLK4 consensus phosphorylation sequence and is positioned close to the known CPAP binding region on STIL (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Cottee et al., 2013; Kettenbach et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2007; Hatzopoulos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 2A and citation (Cottee et al., 2013).

claim: Expression of kinase active PLK4 promoted a > 7 fold increase in the amount of CPAP bound to WT STIL.
source: The expression of kinase active PLK4 promoted a > 7 fold increase in the amount of CPAP bound to WT STIL, but this increased binding was not observed with STIL S428A (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Kinase active PLK4 did not increase CPAP binding to STIL S428A.
source: The expression of kinase active PLK4 promoted a > 7 fold increase in the amount of CPAP bound to WT STIL, but this increased binding was not observed with STIL S428A (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Phosphorylation of WT GST-STIL with PLK4 increased binding to the Flag-TCP domain by ~2.5 fold.
source: Phosphorylation of WT GST-STIL with PLK4 increased binding to the Flag-TCP domain by ~2.5 fold, but this increased binding was not observed with STIL S428A (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phosphorylation of STIL S428A with PLK4 did not increase binding to the Flag-TCP domain.
source: Phosphorylation of WT GST-STIL with PLK4 increased binding to the Flag-TCP domain by ~2.5 fold, but this increased binding was not observed with STIL S428A (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phosphorylation of STIL S428 promotes CPAP binding to STIL in vitro and in vivo.
source: These data show that phosphorylation of STIL S428 promotes CPAP binding to STIL in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The pS428 antibody recognized recombinant GST-STIL in the presence of ATP and the His-PLK4 kinase domain, but not in the absence of ATP.
source: The affinity-purified pS428 antibody recognized recombinant GST-STIL in the presence of ATP and the His-PLK4 kinase domain, but not in the absence of ATP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Recognition of phosphorylated GST-STIL by the pS428 antibody was abolished by the S428A mutation.
source: Moreover, recognition of phosphorylated GST-STIL by the pS428 antibody was abolished by the S428A mutation, demonstrating the specificity of the pS428 antibody (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PLK4 phosphorylates STIL at S428 in vitro and in vivo.
source: The pS428 antibody recognized WT STIL in the presence of kinase active, but not kinase inactive, PLK4, showing that PLK4 phosphorylates STIL at S428 in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: D. melanogaster PLK4 (DmPLK4) phosphorylates the STIL homolog Ana2 at S38, a residue equivalent to S428 in the human STIL.
source: D. melanogaster PLK4 (DmPLK4) was recently shown to phosphorylate the STIL homolog Ana2 at S38, a residue equivalent to S428 in the human STIL (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017; McLamarrah et al., 2018) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017; McLamarrah et al., 2018) and sequence alignment in Figure 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ana2 S38 was shown to be required for Ana2 recruitment.
source: Phosphorylation of S38 was shown to be required for Ana2 recruitment (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017) but was reported to not alter Ana2 binding to the CPAP orthologue DmSas4 (McLamarrah et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017).

claim: Phosphorylation of Ana2 S38 was reported to not alter Ana2 binding to the CPAP orthologue DmSas4.
source: Phosphorylation of S38 was shown to be required for Ana2 recruitment (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017) but was reported to not alter Ana2 binding to the CPAP orthologue DmSas4 (McLamarrah et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation (McLamarrah et al., 2018).

claim: DmPLK4SBM promoted a > 6 fold increase in the amount of DmSas4 bound to WT Ana2.
source: DmPLK4SBM promoted a > 6 fold increase in the amount of DmSas4 bound to WT Ana2, but this increased binding was not observed with Ana2 S38A (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Drosophila S2 cells shown in Figure 2F.

claim: DmPLK4SBM did not increase DmSas4 binding to Ana2 S38A.
source: DmPLK4SBM promoted a > 6 fold increase in the amount of DmSas4 bound to WT Ana2, but this increased binding was not observed with Ana2 S38A (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Drosophila S2 cells shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The increased binding of CPAP/DmSas4 to phosphorylated STIL/Ana2 is conserved between human and flies.
source: These data suggest that the increased binding of CPAP/DmSas4 to phosphorylated STIL/Ana2 is conserved between human and flies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2F.

claim: Depletion of STIL by siRNA for 48 hours resulted in 100% of mitotic cells with ≤2 centrioles.
source: Depletion of STIL by siRNA for 48 hours resulted in 100% of mitotic cells with ≤2 centrioles, and this effect was almost completely rescued by expression of the WT STIL transgene (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) without promoting substantial centriole overduplication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of the WT STIL transgene almost completely rescued the centriole duplication defect caused by STIL depletion.
source: Depletion of STIL by siRNA for 48 hours resulted in 100% of mitotic cells with ≤2 centrioles, and this effect was almost completely rescued by expression of the WT STIL transgene (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) without promoting substantial centriole overduplication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of STIL S428A led to only a partial rescue of centriole duplication (61% S428A cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis).
source: By contrast, expression of either STIL S428A or S1116A only led to a partial rescue of centriole duplication (61% S428A cells and 70% S1116A cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of STIL S1116A led to only a partial rescue of centriole duplication (70% S1116A cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis).
source: By contrast, expression of either STIL S428A or S1116A only led to a partial rescue of centriole duplication (61% S428A cells and 70% S1116A cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Preventing S428 phosphorylation did not affect the ability of STIL to bind to or stimulate PLK4 kinase activity.
source: Importantly, preventing S428 phosphorylation did not affect the ability of STIL to bind to or stimulate PLK4 kinase activity, suggesting that a failure to activate PLK4 kinase activity is not responsible for the failure of centriole duplication (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) (Moyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation of STIL S428 by PLK4 promotes centriole duplication.
source: These data show that phosphorylation of STIL S428 by PLK4 promotes centriole duplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3A.

claim: The STIL PRP mutant showed impaired binding to CPAP.
source: As expected, the STIL PRP mutant showed impaired binding to CPAP (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Expression of Myc-GFP-STIL PRP led to only a partial rescue of centriole duplication in cells depleted of endogenous STIL by siRNA.
source: Expression of Myc-GFP-STIL PRP led to only a partial rescue of centriole duplication in cells depleted of endogenous STIL by siRNA, similar to that of the STIL S428A mutation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Combining the S428A or PRP mutation with the S1116A mutation in the STIL STAN motif prevented any rescue of centriole duplication.
source: Combining the S428A or PRP mutation with the S1116A mutation in the STIL STAN motif that impairs binding to SAS6 prevented any rescue of centriole duplication (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A Myc-GFP-STIL transgene containing both the S428A and PRP mutation rescued centriole duplication to a level similar to that observed with a STIL transgene that contained either mutation on its own.
source: By contrast, a Myc-GFP-STIL transgene containing both the S428A and PRP mutation rescued centriole duplication to a level similar to that observed with a STIL transgene that contained either mutation on its own (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S428 phosphorylation and the PRxxPxP motif of STIL function in the same pathway to promote CPAP binding to STIL.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that S428 phosphorylation and the PRxxPxP motif of STIL function in the same pathway to promote CPAP binding to STIL, and that they both are in a separate pathway from mutations that disrupt SAS6 binding to STIL.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S428 phosphorylation and the PRxxPxP motif of STIL are in a separate pathway from mutations that disrupt SAS6 binding to STIL.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that S428 phosphorylation and the PRxxPxP motif of STIL function in the same pathway to promote CPAP binding to STIL, and that they both are in a separate pathway from mutations that disrupt SAS6 binding to STIL.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Preventing phosphorylation at S428 reduced the localization of Myc-GFP-STIL by 28%, compared to that of the WT transgene.
source: Preventing phosphorylation at S428 reduced the localization of Myc-GFP-STIL by 28%, compared to that of the WT transgene (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of centrosomal STIL levels shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Preventing phosphorylation at S1116 in the STAN motif reduced the abundance of STIL at the centriole by ~2 fold.
source: Preventing phosphorylation at S1116 in the STAN motif reduced the abundance of STIL at the centriole by ~2 fold, as previously reported (Figure 3C) (Moyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of centrosomal STIL levels shown in Figure 3C and citation (Moyer et al., 2015).

claim: Preventing phosphorylation of both S428 and S1116 reduced the centriole localization of STIL by 80%.
source: However, preventing phosphorylation of both sites reduced the centriole localization of STIL by 80%, suggesting that stable incorporation of STIL into the centriole requires strong binding to both CPAP and SAS6 (Figure 3B,C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of centrosomal STIL levels shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stable incorporation of STIL into the centriole requires strong binding to both CPAP and SAS6.
source: However, preventing phosphorylation of both sites reduced the centriole localization of STIL by 80%, suggesting that stable incorporation of STIL into the centriole requires strong binding to both CPAP and SAS6 (Figure 3B,C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effect of mutations at both sites on STIL localization.

claim: Combining the S428A and PRP mutations did not diminish the levels of centriolar STIL below that observed with either mutation alone.
source: Combining the S428A and PRP mutations did not diminish the levels of centriolar STIL below that observed with either mutation alone (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of centrosomal STIL levels shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry promoted phosphorylation of a Myc-GFP-STIL transgene at both S428 and S1116.
source: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry promoted phosphorylation of a Myc-GFP-STIL transgene at both S428 and S1116, and mutation of either site did not prevent phosphorylation of the other (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Mutation of S428 did not prevent phosphorylation of S1116.
source: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry promoted phosphorylation of a Myc-GFP-STIL transgene at both S428 and S1116, and mutation of either site did not prevent phosphorylation of the other (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Mutation of S1116 did not prevent phosphorylation of S428.
source: Expression of kinase active PLK4∆24-mCherry promoted phosphorylation of a Myc-GFP-STIL transgene at both S428 and S1116, and mutation of either site did not prevent phosphorylation of the other (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Treatment with the PLK4 inhibitor centrinone abolished STIL S1108 phosphorylation.
source: Although treatment with the PLK4 inhibitor centrinone abolished STIL S1108 phosphorylation, the S428A or PRP motif mutation did not affect phosphorylation of STIL S1108 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The S428A or PRP motif mutation did not affect phosphorylation of STIL S1108.
source: Although treatment with the PLK4 inhibitor centrinone abolished STIL S1108 phosphorylation, the S428A or PRP motif mutation did not affect phosphorylation of STIL S1108 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Phosphorylation of the STIL STAN motif by PLK4 does not require prior phosphorylation of STIL S428.
source: These data show that phosphorylation of the STIL STAN motif by PLK4 does not require prior phosphorylation of STIL S428.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Myc-GFP-STIL WT partially recovered following bleaching in FRAP experiments (recovery percentage (R%)=38%).
source: Myc-GFP-STIL WT partially recovered following bleaching, showing that STIL exists in both mobile and immobile pool at the procentriole (Figure 4A, Myc-GFP-STIL WT, recovery percentage (R%)=38%).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: STIL exists in both mobile and immobile pool at the procentriole.
source: Myc-GFP-STIL WT partially recovered following bleaching, showing that STIL exists in both mobile and immobile pool at the procentriole (Figure 4A, Myc-GFP-STIL WT, recovery percentage (R%)=38%).
evidence: This is inferred from the partial recovery observed in FRAP experiments.

claim: Mutation of the S1116 phosphorylation site increased the mobile fraction of centriolar STIL (R% = 71%).
source: Consistent with previous observations, mutation of the S1116 phosphorylation site increased the mobile fraction of centriolar STIL (Figure 4A, Myc-GFP-STIL S1116A, R% = 71%) (Moyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4A and citation (Moyer et al., 2015).

claim: The S428A mutant of STIL showed an increased recovery of centriolar STIL (R% = 57%).
source: Importantly, the S428A and PRP mutants of STIL also showed an increased recovery of centriolar STIL (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1); Myc-GFP-STIL S428A, R% = 57%; Myc-GFP-STIL PRP, R% = 58%), suggesting that CPAP binding allows more stable incorporation of STIL into the procentriole.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The PRP mutant of STIL showed an increased recovery of centriolar STIL (R% = 58%).
source: Importantly, the S428A and PRP mutants of STIL also showed an increased recovery of centriolar STIL (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1); Myc-GFP-STIL S428A, R% = 57%; Myc-GFP-STIL PRP, R% = 58%), suggesting that CPAP binding allows more stable incorporation of STIL into the procentriole.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CPAP binding allows more stable incorporation of STIL into the procentriole.
source: Importantly, the S428A and PRP mutants of STIL also showed an increased recovery of centriolar STIL (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1); Myc-GFP-STIL S428A, R% = 57%; Myc-GFP-STIL PRP, R% = 58%), suggesting that CPAP binding allows more stable incorporation of STIL into the procentriole.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased turnover of STIL mutants that cannot bind CPAP.

claim: Myc-GFP-CPAP partially recovered after photobleaching (R% = 51%).
source: As previously reported, Myc-GFP-CPAP partially recovered after photobleaching (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), Myc-GFP-CPAP, R% = 51%) (Kitagawa et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and citation (Kitagawa et al., 2011b).

claim: Depletion of STIL led to an almost complete turnover of Myc-GFP-CPAP (R% = 96%).
source: Surprisingly, performing the same measurements in cells depleted of STIL led to an almost complete turnover of Myc-GFP-CPAP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Myc-GFP-CPAP, STIL siRNA, R% = 96%).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: STIL is required for the stable incorporation of CPAP at the procentriole.
source: Since we bleach all of the pools of CPAP in the FRAP experiments, we cannot distinguish which centrosomal populations of CPAP are dynamic and which are stably bound. Nevertheless, given STIL localizes exclusively to the procentriole, one interpretation of our data is that STIL is required for the stable incorporation of CPAP at the procentriole, while the parental centriole and PCM pool of CPAP are dynamic and display a more transient association with the centrosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data showing increased CPAP turnover upon STIL depletion.

claim: The parental centriole and PCM pool of CPAP are dynamic and display a more transient association with the centrosome.
source: Since we bleach all of the pools of CPAP in the FRAP experiments, we cannot distinguish which centrosomal populations of CPAP are dynamic and which are stably bound. Nevertheless, given STIL localizes exclusively to the procentriole, one interpretation of our data is that STIL is required for the stable incorporation of CPAP at the procentriole, while the parental centriole and PCM pool of CPAP are dynamic and display a more transient association with the centrosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data and the localization patterns of STIL and CPAP.

claim: Mutation of S428 or the PRP motif on STIL increased the turnover of GFP-CPAP compared with WT STIL.
source: However, mutation of S428 or the PRP motif on STIL increased the turnover of GFP-CPAP compared with WT STIL (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, GFP-CPAP, Myc-STIL S428A background, R% = 69%; GFP-CPAP, Myc-STIL PRP background, R% = 67%).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of Myc-STIL S1116A did not increase GFP-CPAP turnover.
source: Expression of Myc-STIL S1116A did not increase GFP-CPAP turnover, indicating that the increase in GFP-CPAP turnover in a Myc-STIL S428A background reflects a specific defect in the STIL/CPAP interaction (Figure 4B, GFP-CPAP, Myc-STIL S1116A background, R% = 55%).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: STIL binding allows a more stable incorporation of CPAP into the centrosome.
source: These data suggest that STIL binding allows a more stable incorporation of CPAP into the centrosome, possibly by facilitating interactions with CPAP at the procentriole.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data showing increased CPAP turnover when STIL-CPAP interaction is disrupted.

claim: STIL recruits additional proteins that collectively act to stabilize the incorporation of CPAP into the centrosome.
source: However, since the depletion of STIL resulted in a higher level of CPAP turnover than specifically disrupting the STIL/CPAP interaction, it is likely STIL recruits additional proteins that collectively act to stabilize the incorporation of CPAP into the centrosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that STIL depletion has a stronger effect on CPAP turnover than disrupting the STIL-CPAP interaction.

claim: The interaction of CPAP with STIL allows both proteins to incorporate more stably into the centrosome.
source: Together, our data show that the interaction of CPAP with STIL allows both proteins to incorporate more stably into the centrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Knockdown of CPAP by siRNA resulted in 81% of mitotic cells with ≤2 centrioles.
source: Knockdown of CPAP by siRNA resulted in 81% of mitotic cells with ≤2 centrioles, and this was largely rescued by expression of the CPAP WT transgene (Figure 5C) without promoting centriole overduplication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of the CPAP WT transgene largely rescued the centriole duplication defect caused by CPAP depletion.
source: Knockdown of CPAP by siRNA resulted in 81% of mitotic cells with ≤2 centrioles, and this was largely rescued by expression of the CPAP WT transgene (Figure 5C) without promoting centriole overduplication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of a CPAP transgene with F1229A mutation led to a partial rescue of centriole duplication (58% of F1229A cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis).
source: By contrast, expression of a CPAP transgene with mutations in the TCP domain that reduced binding to STIL (F1229A or E1235K), led to a partial rescue of centriole duplication (58% of F1229A cells and 48% of E1235K cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis) (Figure 5C, Figure 5D) (Cottee et al., 2013; Hatzopoulos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of a CPAP transgene with E1235K mutation led to a partial rescue of centriole duplication (48% of E1235K cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis).
source: By contrast, expression of a CPAP transgene with mutations in the TCP domain that reduced binding to STIL (F1229A or E1235K), led to a partial rescue of centriole duplication (58% of F1229A cells and 48% of E1235K cells contain ≤2 centrioles in mitosis) (Figure 5C, Figure 5D) (Cottee et al., 2013; Hatzopoulos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The presence of F1229A or E1235K TCP domain mutations increased the turnover of Myc-GFP-CPAP at the centrosome.
source: Importantly, the presence of these TCP domain mutations increased the turnover of Myc-GFP-CPAP at the centrosome (Figure 5E, Myc-GFP-CPAP R% = 51%; Myc-GFP-CPAP F1229A, R% = 76%; Myc-GFP-CPAP E1235K, R% = 67%), but did not alter the abundance of the Myc-GFP-CPAP or STIL at the centrosome (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The F1229A or E1235K TCP domain mutations did not alter the abundance of Myc-GFP-CPAP or STIL at the centrosome.
source: Importantly, the presence of these TCP domain mutations increased the turnover of Myc-GFP-CPAP at the centrosome (Figure 5E, Myc-GFP-CPAP R% = 51%; Myc-GFP-CPAP F1229A, R% = 76%; Myc-GFP-CPAP E1235K, R% = 67%), but did not alter the abundance of the Myc-GFP-CPAP or STIL at the centrosome (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The STIL-CPAP interaction facilitates the stable centrosomal integration of CPAP.
source: Collectively, these data support the conclusion that the STIL-CPAP interaction facilitates the stable centrosomal integration of CPAP, but that this interaction does not have a major impact on the level to which CPAP accumulates at the centrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The STIL-CPAP interaction does not have a major impact on the level to which CPAP accumulates at the centrosome.
source: Collectively, these data support the conclusion that the STIL-CPAP interaction facilitates the stable centrosomal integration of CPAP, but that this interaction does not have a major impact on the level to which CPAP accumulates at the centrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5F-H.

claim: STIL knockdown reduced the level of CPAP at the centrosome by ~30%.
source: STIL knockdown reduced the level of CPAP at the centrosome by ~30% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Centrosomal CPAP levels were similar following depletion of endogenous STIL and expression of a WT or mutant Myc-GFP-STIL transgene.
source: Importantly, we observed that centrosomal CPAP levels were similar following depletion of endogenous STIL and expression of a WT or mutant Myc-GFP-STIL transgene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: CPAP is localized to the parent centriole independently of STIL.
source: This suggests a model in which CPAP is localized to the parent centriole independently of STIL, while procentriole localized CPAP requires STIL for stable binding.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: Procentriole localized CPAP requires STIL for stable binding.
source: This suggests a model in which CPAP is localized to the parent centriole independently of STIL, while procentriole localized CPAP requires STIL for stable binding.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: The role of STIL in recruiting CPAP to the centrosome is largely independent of the STIL/CPAP interaction.
source: However, our data argue that the role of STIL in recruiting CPAP to the centrosome is largely independent of the STIL/CPAP interaction and likely depends on the recruitment of other proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that STIL depletion has a stronger effect on CPAP levels than disrupting the STIL-CPAP interaction.

claim: The recruitment of the majority of CPAP present at the centrosome does not require CPAP binding to STIL.
source: We conclude that the recruitment of the majority of CPAP present at the centrosome does not require CPAP binding to STIL.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of STIL suppressed de novo centriole assembly.
source: As expected, depletion of STIL suppressed de novo centriole assembly, and this was rescued by expression of a WT Myc-GFP-STIL transgene (48% and 87% of cells expressing WT STIL contained de novo centrioles at 24 and 72 hr after centrinone washout, respectively) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of a WT Myc-GFP-STIL transgene rescued de novo centriole assembly (48% and 87% of cells expressing WT STIL contained de novo centrioles at 24 and 72 hr after centrinone washout, respectively).
source: As expected, depletion of STIL suppressed de novo centriole assembly, and this was rescued by expression of a WT Myc-GFP-STIL transgene (48% and 87% of cells expressing WT STIL contained de novo centrioles at 24 and 72 hr after centrinone washout, respectively) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Acentriolar cell lines expressing S428A, S1116A, or PRP Myc-GFP-STIL were all deficient in assembling de novo centrioles.
source: Acentriolar cell lines expressing a S428A, S1116A, or PRP Myc-GFP-STIL transgene were all deficient in assembling de novo centrioles, with only 25%, 12%, and 33% of cells containing PLK4 and Centrin positive foci at 72 hr after centrinone removal, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cells expressing S1116A Myc-GFP-STIL formed very few GFP-STIL/PLK4 foci.
source: While cells expressing S1116A Myc-GFP-STIL formed very few GFP-STIL/PLK4 foci, the number of foci observed in cells expressing S428A and PRP Myc-GFP-STIL was comparable to that observed with the WT STIL transgene (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The number of GFP-STIL/PLK4 foci in cells expressing S428A and PRP Myc-GFP-STIL was comparable to that observed with the WT STIL transgene.
source: While cells expressing S1116A Myc-GFP-STIL formed very few GFP-STIL/PLK4 foci, the number of foci observed in cells expressing S428A and PRP Myc-GFP-STIL was comparable to that observed with the WT STIL transgene (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cells expressing the S428A and PRP mutant STIL fail centriole assembly at a later stage than those expressing the S1116A mutant of STIL.
source: This suggests that cells expressing the S428A and PRP mutant STIL fail centriole assembly at a later stage than those expressing the S1116A mutant of STIL.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that S428A and PRP mutants form STIL/PLK4 foci but fail to complete centriole assembly.

claim: WT Myc-GFP-STIL recruited both CPAP and SAS6 to de novo centrioles.
source: WT Myc-GFP-STIL recruited both CPAP and SAS6 to as expected (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-H.

claim: Recruitment of SAS6 was identical in WT, S428A, and PRP Myc-GFP-STIL.
source: While recruitment of SAS6 was identical in WT, S428A, and PRP Myc-GFP-STIL, the S428A and PRP mutations resulted in a > 90% reduction in the amount of CPAP recruitment to the GFP-STIL/PLK4 foci (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The S428A and PRP mutations resulted in a > 90% reduction in the amount of CPAP recruitment to the GFP-STIL/PLK4 foci.
source: While recruitment of SAS6 was identical in WT, S428A, and PRP Myc-GFP-STIL, the S428A and PRP mutations resulted in a > 90% reduction in the amount of CPAP recruitment to the GFP-STIL/PLK4 foci (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: S428A and PRP mutant STIL bind to SAS6 and assemble a cartwheel but fail to recruit CPAP to complete the formation of de novo centrioles.
source: Together, these data suggest that S428A and PRP mutant STIL bind to SAS6 and assemble a cartwheel but fail to recruit CPAP to complete the formation of de novo centrioles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Active PLK4 phosphorylates STIL at the site of procentriole assembly in two different regions with distinct functional consequences.
source: Our data lead us to propose a model whereby active PLK4 phosphorylates STIL at the site of procentriole assembly in two different regions with distinct functional consequences (Figure 7): phosphorylation of multiple residues in the STAN motif, most notably S1116, allows STIL binding to SAS6 to promote cartwheel assembly. Second, phosphorylation of S428 promotes the binding of the STIL PRP motif to CPAP, thereby linking the growing cartwheel to the triplet microtubules of the centriole wall.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation of S428 promotes the binding of the STIL PRP motif to CPAP, thereby linking the growing cartwheel to the triplet microtubules of the centriole wall.
source: Our data lead us to propose a model whereby active PLK4 phosphorylates STIL at the site of procentriole assembly in two different regions with distinct functional consequences (Figure 7): phosphorylation of multiple residues in the STAN motif, most notably S1116, allows STIL binding to SAS6 to promote cartwheel assembly. Second, phosphorylation of S428 promotes the binding of the STIL PRP motif to CPAP, thereby linking the growing cartwheel to the triplet microtubules of the centriole wall.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Super-resolution imaging of Drosophila centrioles has revealed that the C-terminal region of Ana2/STIL containing the STAN motif is located closer to the cartwheel hub.
source: Moreover, super-resolution imaging of Drosophila centrioles has revealed that the C-terminal region of Ana2/STIL containing the STAN motif is located closer to the cartwheel hub, while the N-terminal region containing the PRP motif is positioned close to the C-terminus of Sas-4/CPAP at the periphery of the cartwheel (Gartenmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Gartenmann et al., 2017).

claim: The N-terminal region of Ana2/STIL containing the PRP motif is positioned close to the C-terminus of Sas-4/CPAP at the periphery of the cartwheel.
source: Moreover, super-resolution imaging of Drosophila centrioles has revealed that the C-terminal region of Ana2/STIL containing the STAN motif is located closer to the cartwheel hub, while the N-terminal region containing the PRP motif is positioned close to the C-terminus of Sas-4/CPAP at the periphery of the cartwheel (Gartenmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Gartenmann et al., 2017).

claim: A mutation in the CPAP TCP domain that causes microcephaly in humans has been shown to decrease the affinity of CPAP to STIL.
source: A mutation in the CPAP TCP domain that causes microcephaly in humans has been shown to decrease the affinity of CPAP to STIL (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Bond et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Cottee et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2011; Bond et al., 2005).

claim: Mutations in STIL that reside in the CPAP and SAS6 interacting motifs have been identified in patients with microcephaly.
source: Also, mutations in STIL that reside in the CPAP and SAS6 interacting motifs have also been identified in patients with microcephaly, although the significance of these alterations remains to be determined (Cristofoli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Cristofoli et al., 2017).

claim: Recruitment of CPAP to assembling de novo centrioles requires STIL S428 phosphorylation.
source: Although recruitment of CPAP to assembling de novo centrioles requires STIL S428 phosphorylation, this modification is not required for recruiting the bulk of CPAP to the centrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: STIL S428 phosphorylation is not required for recruiting the bulk of CPAP to the centrosome.
source: Although recruitment of CPAP to assembling de novo centrioles requires STIL S428 phosphorylation, this modification is not required for recruiting the bulk of CPAP to the centrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: De novo centriole assembly may have some distinct requirements compared with canonical centriole biogenesis.
source: We envisage two possible explanations for this discrepancy. First, although sharing obvious similarities, de novo centriole assembly may have some distinct requirements compared with canonical centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the observed differences.

claim: Multiple pools of CPAP at the centrosome may obscure the ability to accurately monitor the role of STIL phosphorylation in CPAP recruitment at the nascent procentriole.
source: A second possibility is that multiple pools of CPAP at the centrosome (parent centriole, procentriole and PCM associated) may obscure the ability to accurately monitor the role of STIL phosphorylation in CPAP recruitment at the nascent procentriole.
evidence: This is speculation about possible technical limitations.

claim: Even if the STIL-CPAP interaction is not strictly necessary for the recruitment of either protein to canonically duplicating centrioles, it does allow for the more stable integration of these proteins into the centrosome.
source: In any case, it is clear that even if the STIL-CPAP interaction is not strictly necessary for the recruitment of either protein to canonically duplicating centrioles, it does allow for the more stable integration of these proteins into the centrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation of S428 may create an extended binding interface that increases the affinity of STIL to CPAP.
source: We envisage two, non-mutually exclusive possibilities. First, phosphorylation creates an extended binding interface that increases the affinity of STIL to CPAP.
evidence: This is speculation about possible molecular mechanisms.

claim: Sequence conservation in the CPAP TCP domain extends beyond the region that directly interacts with the PRP motif of STIL.
source: Indeed, sequence conservation in the CPAP TCP domain is not confined to the region that directly interacts with the PRP motif of STIL, but extends further along the surface of the TCP domain beta sheet, suggesting that additional contacts with STIL may occur in this region (Cottee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Cottee et al., 2013).

claim: There is high conservation around the S428 phosphorylation site on STIL.
source: Moreover, there is high conservation around the S428 phosphorylation site on STIL, and this conserved motif was proposed to be well positioned to form an extended interaction interface with conserved residues in the CPAP TCP domain (Cottee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data and citation (Cottee et al., 2013).

claim: Phosphorylation of STIL S428 could generate a conformational change that unmasks the PRP motif in STIL and exposes it for binding to CPAP.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that S428 phosphorylation generates a conformational change that unmasks the PRP motif in STIL and exposes it for binding to CPAP.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative molecular mechanism.

claim: Phosphorylation of the homologous site (S38) on Ana2/STIL leads to a dramatic mobility shift in an SDS page gel that is likely to reflect a significant conformational change in Ana2.
source: In support of this model, work in Drosophila has shown that phosphorylation of the homologous site (S38) on Ana2/STIL leads to a dramatic mobility shift in an SDS page gel that is likely to reflect a significant conformational change in Ana2 (Dzhindzhev et al., 2017).

claim: C. elegans SAS-5/STIL lacks an obvious PRP motif.
